Kuṟuntokai 88. Maturaik Katakkaṇṇaṉ: the confidante / SHE
Kuṟuntokai 130. Veḷḷi Vīti(yār): the confidante / SHE

lg.l: [The hero’s] consideration of [the heroine and confidante’s] closeness;
[The hero] expressing his desire [for a meeting] entreatingly when [her friend has] doubts;

[the confidante] then questioning [the hero]; [the hero] creating a mutual understanding;In practice, this means that the hero makes the confidante aware of his relationship with the heroine. Here it is understood as him bringing their minds together, i.e., creating an understanding, but it is explained slightly differently in the IAC. There, the confidante’s knowledge has been split, so she knows that her friend is suffering, but that knowledge is split from its cause, the hero. His actions in this situation reconcile that split and make the confidante aware of their relationship.
[the confidante] determining [the intention of the hero]; [the confidante] putting [the hero] at a distance;
[the confidante] saying, ‘Do not hide being one who knows [by saying] that you do not know what is pointed out’;
[the confidante] speaking [to him about] what is not intended; [the confidante] making things up;
[the confidante] saying she is difficult [to approach]; [the confidante] saying, ‘You speak [to her]’;
[the confidante] jokingly comforting [the hero]; [the hero] saying, ‘Speak [to me] without joking’;
[the confidante] saying, ‘You great man, we are not appropriate for that’;
[the confidante] demonstrating the uniqueness of the gift;This is not in praise of the gift, but rather highlighting the fact that it is not unique.
[the confidante] saying, ‘It is not suitable to touch [her] body’;
[the confidante] saying, ‘Knowing her state, I will take [the gift]’; speaking of the Palmyra horse;
[the confidante] opposing [it]; [the confidante] accepting the gift;
[the confidante] speaking [to the heroine] entreatingly [on his behalf]; [the confidante speaking of the hero] leaving in shame;
[the confidante] persuading [the heroine] to accept [the hero’s] request by speaking forcefully;
[the confidante] kindly accepting [the leaf skirt]; [the confidante] entrusting the leaf skirt [to the heroine];
[the heroine] accepting the gift; [the confidante] saying [to the hero] that [the acceptance of the gift] had come true;
speaking about the desired [meeting-]place; [the confidante] leaving with [knowledge of] the tryst;

[the] hero standing [there] having decorated [the heroine];My instinct is to understand this as the heroine standing, ready to be picked up, after the hero had helped her get ready after their tryst. The Tamil, however, suggests the hero ought to be the agent of both verbs. puṉai-tal is a transitive root, and it is clear from the poem quoted in the commentary for this situation that the heroine is not the one who decorated herself, but that it was the hero. [the hero] speaking [to the confidante] about [the heroine’s] state;
[the heroine’s] friend taking [her] and leaving – [these] are [the situations of] the daytime tryst.

div.p: e-tu. tōḻiyiṟ kūṭṭattup pakaṟ kuṟi yām āṟuṇarttutaṉutaliṟṟu.
The quoted [cūttiram] intends to make known the way in which the daytime meeting place for a union [by means of] the confidante occurs.
pāṅkiyai yuṇarntatu mutal ākak koṇṭu peyarntatīṟākac collap paṭṭaṉa vellān tōḻiyiṉ ākiya pakaṟ kuṟik kūṭṭam ām eṉṟa vāṟu.

Beginning with ‘considering her friend’ and ending with ‘[the confidante] taking [the heroine] and departing’, all of the things mentioned are the union at the daytime meeting place on account of the confidante.

lg.l: The girl with the beautiful jewels has a dear friend
who is like her sweet life because of the love she has [for her]

– aṉṉa is understood to introduce an example. If punctuated differently, ‘for example’ or ‘such as’. if [the heroine] looks [around], she does not look at other faces,The two -iṉum clauses are understood here as co-ordinated conditionals enumerating the friend’s behaviour across different situations. They can also be read as concessives: ‘even if [the heroine] looks [around]… even if [the heroine] approaches…’. In either case, the subject of nōkkiṉum can be the confidante herself, the heroine, or others, while the confidante remains the subject of nōkkāḷ. The same applies to cāriṉum. The point in all readings is the same: the friend’s attention is fixed on the heroine and they are inseparable.
if the young woman with flowers in her hair approaches [somewhere],
[her friend] will be joined to her shoulder.

div.p: eṉpatu pāṅkiyai yuṇarntatu.
This is [the hero] having considered the confidante.In both the AV and KK, this poem is quoted to illustrate an earlier stage in the relationship. In both cases it is cited in iyaṟkaip puṇarcci.

lg.l: Even though she throws around flower-balls with her friends decorated with jewels,

and even though she plucks the bright mature flowers of the ñāḻal bloomed from buds,naṉai malar ñāḻal could be taken differently. naṉai is also a verbal root (‘to be wet’) and could qualify the malar (‘blossom/flower’), though why exactly this would be the case is not totally clear. It is a neytal plant (see the commentary to TNV 12), so it would be in proximity to the sea. Understanding it as ‘buds’, I think the ‘mature flowers’ she plucks make a nice counterpart, and were probably what the poet intended.
Is that distinctive colour not spreading on the young woman?

div.p: eṉpatu vēṟu pāṭu kaṇṭu pāṅki yaiyuṟṟatu.
This is her friend having expressed doubt after seeing the changes [in the heroine’s state].

lg.l: The qualities of the chaplet are superior
and the leaf skirt of cool flowers seems just right.cevviya refers to something happening at the opportune moment. In this case, the flowers for the leaf skirt were picked at the right time.
So that [her] curly dark hair and hips shine.

Take it, you eminent one!ēntiṉir can also mean ‘to hold, carry’ or ‘to stretch out one’s hands’. Thus this phrase could be translated as: ‘Hold out your hands and take it so that…’, or something very similar. How greatly weThe hero quite regularly uses the royal ‘we’ when talking about himself. In some cases one can reasonably assume (or it is obvious) that ‘we’ refers to him and his heart, though there is nothing to suggest that is the case here. Perhaps the idea is to make him sound pompous. This poem is essentially him pathetically self-aggrandising. desire that!

div.p: eṉpatu talaimakaṉ irantu kuṟai yuṟṟatu.
This is the hero having entreatingly expressed [his] desire.

lg.l: Day after day, O lord, you come this way holding gifts.
Besides that, what we do not know is:
if we speak to our family,
will you obtain our father’s great generosity?In other words: ‘will our father accept you?’.

div.p: eṉpatu talaimakaṉait tōḻi viṉāyiṟṟu.
This is the confidante having questioned the hero.

lg.l: Were there stags with open hot wounds,vāya – an adjectival form of vāy – can also be understood as ‘a mouth’. In which case, we can translate: ‘stags with mouths with hot wounds…’. I do not find either interpretation particularly more plausible than the other.
split open by arrow-heads, that came by,

thinking ofThe other older meaning of paṭar-tal is ‘to set off’. One could also take this phrase as: ‘setting off to join with…’. joining with your doe-like glances?maṭam māṉ nōkkam can also be understood as an aṉmoḻittokai, referring to the heroine and confidante as ‘[you with] the doe-like glances’. One could then either keep the phrase as the object of maruvutal, or construe the sentence differently and read it as a vocative, and have an elliptical object for the verb.

div.p: eṉpatu kavarntu niṉṟa tōḻiyai mati yuṭaṉ paṭuppāṉ uṟṟut tōḻiyun talaimakaḷum uṭaṉ āya vaḻit talaimakaṉ viṉāyatu.
This is the hero having questioned the confidante and the heroine while they were together in order to bring the confidante’s mind together [with his own], after grabbing [her attention].

lg.l: Please tell meIt is uncommon to find the particle -maṉ affixed to an imperative and it is not entirely clear what its exact nuance is. Cf. Kali 93.10 and Kali 108.20. the way through the mountains,

that, having passed the difficult, distressing crossroads,Whether to take paṭar as a noun or a verbal root will change how one construes the poem. As understood in the translation, it is a noun meaning ‘affliction/distress’ in attributive position, qualifying the crossroads. As a verbal root, it could function as a peyareccam, in which case the crossroads might be ‘difficult to pass’.

brings onepeyar taru is analysed here as an auxiliary construction, where peyar-tal makes an action outside of the control of the agent. In this case it ‘brings [one] to move’. Theoretically, one could understand the opposite, as peyar-tal means both ‘to depart’ and ‘to return’. to the fortAs suggested by the TL, though only with reference to an entry in the Piṅkalam, perhaps this can refer to a town. One would expect the hero here to be asking for the way to the heroine’s village. The meaning of town has no early poetic attestation and the common meaning in the early corpus is ‘fort’ (cf. PN 224.1), which also makes sense, though it is a departure from the topos as found in the PK. Perhaps the connotation is that the heroine’s town is a protected settlement. of great suffering.

div.p: eṉpatu vaḻi viṉāyatu.
This is [the hero] having asked about the way.

lg.l: In his hands wasLit.: ‘the thing in his hands was the…’. the pretty aśoka leaf skirt
and he asked afterLit.: ‘the thing he asked after was…’. the stags with wounds in their mouths.
Alas! He does not let go and leave the wide field.
We don’t know anything about what this worthy man is thinking.

div.p: eṉpatu talaimakaṉait tōḻi yaiyuṟṟatu.
This is the confidante having doubted [the intentions of] the hero.

lg.l: The man from the land where groups of peacocks climb
the flowering branches of the kino tree and call out

– he has in his mind the vine-like woman with the bright forehead.One could also understand that he is on the mind of the heroine. As he has been the speaker in the previous situations, it is more likely that the confidante understands something about his intentions. The koḷu also allows for this ambiguity.

div.p: eṉpatu tōḻi talaimakaṉait tuṇintatu.
This is the confidante having determined [the intentions of] the hero.

lg.l: Approaching the cool slope is difficult.

If there is a request that [you] consider,Or, possibly: ‘If there is a request to be considered [by you]’. In this case, the poem would read as a slightly long-winded way to ask the hero to keep his distance. The normal subtext of this situation, however, is that the hero ought to let the confidante accomplish his request rather than keep hanging around, trying to organise the tryst himself.
you shall complete it without approaching [here], your majesty.

div.p: eṉpatu talaimakaṉaic cēṭpaṭa niṟuttatu.
This is [the confidante] having put the hero at a distance.

lg.l: Amongst the women with honey-scented hair
busy playing toy houses on the curved dark mountainside,
what might have become of [your] lord’s sweet grace?aruḷ can also mean ‘consideration’, in which case the poem could have a slightly different flavour, but only very slightly.

div.p: eṉpatu aṟiyāḷ pōṉṟatu.
This is the confidante having appeared not to know [the hero’s intentions].

lg.l: The one with the grace of a peacock and a bright forehead
who seized your good heartMore literally: ‘heart with good qualities’ or ‘meritorious heart’. on the slope full of flowers

– she is one who loves us as though [our] lives are one.It is not immediately obvious who the objects of the heroine’s love are, apart from the confidante. The use of the exclusive first person plural clearly indicates that the hero, to whom this speech is addressed, is not included. Presumably this then refers to either her group of friends or her family. Unless the pronoun is not intended to be exclusive, this is either a departure from the topos found in the PK, where the confidante realises the hero and heroine are as though one, or a different topos. Another option, though not one that solves this problem, is to understand aṉpiṉaḷ as ‘who is beloved’, in which case the confidante is explaining that the heroine is dear to her (and whoever else is the referent of the pronoun).

div.p: eṉpatu aṟiyak kūṟiyatu.
This is [the confidante] having declared knowingly.

lg.l: O lord with the sharp spear, if you hide from her friendsayam is very polysemous and the oblique here can also be understood in more than one way. Either he is hiding his intention from her friends, which is close to the situation found in the PK where he hides it from the confidante, or he is literally hiding amongst the herders on the mountain. On the strength of the similarity to the PK, the first translation is preferred.
with the sweet-smelling chaplets on the tall mountain,
the task you have in mind will not be completed.

div.p: eṉpatu maṟaiyēl eṉṟatu.
This is [the confidante] having said, ‘Do not hide!’ [to the hero].

lg.l: Like MatitaraṉThis is the only proper name in any of the poems cited in this commentary. UVC suggests in his introduction to the 1937 first edition that this might be the name of the author’s teacher. with a truthful tongue

who appeared in the ancient clanThis could either be referring to him appearing in the clan, i.e., being born into an illustrious ancient lineage, or to him appearing in front of them, though what that would mean is less clear. full of purity

is the great shining mountain that stands immovableThis might be a play on words. Not only is Matitaraṉ (lit. ‘one who supports the moon’) steadfast, but in the same way that a tall mountain might appear to hold up the moon, so, by virtue of his name, does he.
as the ascetics, superior in their penance, approach.

div.p: eṉpatu tōḻi talaimakaṉ kuṟiyātatu kūṟiyatu.
This is the confidante having told the hero about something he did not intend [to discuss].

lg.l: My people – the strong men with cruel bows –
will come this way with murderous rage.More literally: ‘with rage [that is] the task/action of murder’.
So go, O man from the mountainside! [This] brings harm.Lit.: ‘This possesses harm-bringing’.

div.p: eṉpatu tōḻi paṭaittu moḻintatu.
This is the confidante having made things up.

lg.l: She is not chasing crabs, or playing toy houses
with her friendsāyamoṭu could alternatively be taken with either the toy house game or chasing crabs. In this translation, it applies to both. in the seashore-grove where flowers blossom.
She is like a painted doll.
Howyātukol… āṟu is literally ‘in what way’. This allows for the possibility of both: ‘how can I speak?’ and ‘what should I say?’. can I speak to her, O lord?

div.p: ituvum atu.
And this is that.

lg.l: O man from the shining mountain range,
where from atop the great mountain
long white waterfalls cascade down the mountainside,
resounding like the drums of the drummers
with ancient wisdom – pain is appropriate.
for those who do not know what is good.

div.p: ituvum atu.
And this is that.

lg.l: Since you came recently, you don’t understand.

Oh, she is not easy [to reach] at the opportune moment.The semantic nuance here is not clear. This translation has taken the common dictionary definition for paṭam, ‘right moment’, and has extrapolated that into the heroine being difficult to pin down. It could also have another nuance such as expressing an idea of appropriateness, in which case she would be difficult to approach because the confidante is unworthy of her time. In either case, the heroine is difficult to approach. A third option would be to understand paṭam as the Sanskrit pada, in which case it could mean ‘rank, station’. The line would then read: ‘O, she is not easy [to reach] for [those of] our station!’ Purely in terms of sense, this might be the cleanest interpretation, but the TNV is generally not a very Sanskritic text.
The young woman is just like a godiyavuḷ is seemingly a novel usage. The affixed assertive particle -maṉ is rendered as ‘just’. [to our] lives here.

div.p: eṉpatu talaimakaḷ ariyaḷ eṉṟatu.
This is [the confidante] having said [to the hero], ‘She is difficult [to speak to]’.

lg.l: O lord with a shining spear like a flash of lightning,
you tell the young woman, whose soft breasts

have beauty spots golden in nature,It could also be that the beauty spots are another attribute of the heroine and not located specifically on her breasts. There is no clear way to know from the Tamil.

div.p: eṉpatu niṉkuṟai nīyē kūṟeṉṟatu.
This is [the confidante] having told [the hero], ‘Tell [the heroine] your request yourself!’

lg.l: Oh, there can only be one intention!
That young woman with bangles on her forearm
– what of her very ownThe final tāṉ is understood as an emphatic – ‘what of that very smile?’ or something similar. budding smile

in which teeth appear like sprouts?To avoid the repetition of ‘bud’, arumpiya is translated as ‘appear’. The image is that her smile is budding in the sense that her teeth are still coming in and that they literally resemble fresh white sprouts.

div.p: eṉpatu nakai koṇṭāṟṟal.
This is [the confidante] comforting [the hero] jokingly.

lg.l: You who are studied in the ways of obtaining [her],Could one also take peṟu tiṟam nāṭiṉai as ‘you who know the issue at hand’, or something similar? Understanding tiṟam as ‘issue’ is unproblematic, but this interpretation might stretch the range of peṟu-tal.

without joking,nakāatu could qualify uṟu tuyar, in which case it would mean: ‘the unjoking/unsmiling experience of misery’. The reason it is translated as such is because of the speech situation. speak of the way to live besides in misery
on account of the girlmātar is unmarked for case and it could reasonably be understood differently: ‘in misery with the woman…’, for example. with the fragrant forehead who wears bangles.

div.p: eṉpatu nakāturai yeṉṟatu.
This is [the hero] having said [to the confidante], ‘Speak without joking!’

lg.l: For us from a small hamlet living unsophisticatedThe general thrust of tiruntā is clear – the confidante and heroine are lower in status than the hero. Its exact nuance is a little unclear: are they untrained? imperfect? unworthy? lives,

O most worthy lord, is even a suitable friendshipBoth poruntiya and kēṇmai can be taken differently, as the peyareccam of ‘come together’ and as ‘intimacy’, respectively. The relationship in question would then be one of close intimacy, and would most likely necessitate a slightly different understanding of the -um particle; perhaps as carrying the force of ‘at all’ or ‘any’, in which case: ‘would any intimate friendship with you…’.

with you great? It is not!puraivatō aṉṟē can be understood differently. One can take purai as a verbal root meaning ‘to resemble’, which is how some translators of this poem have understood this (see Buck and Paramasivan 1997), in which case the point is that the heroine’s life does not resemble that of the hero, thus making their relationship unsuitable. emakku in line one makes that read less smoothly. Another option would be to understand purai as a verbal root meaning ‘to be suitable’, in which case the question is whether such a relationship would be appropriate for the girls. The interpretation makes good sense, but this meaning is not well attested in the old corpus. In NA 45.10 and NA 238.7, the question and answer clearly seem to be ‘is x great? It is not’. I feel confident the poet was referencing this, so I keep that meaning.

div.p: eṉpatu yām umakkiyaiyō meṉṟatu.
This is [the confidante] having said, ‘We are not suitable for you.’

lg.l: Do the women with cloud-like locks

really pound pearlsThis may have been for some sort of cosmetic preparation. From a quite superficial internet search for ‘pearl powder’, it seems as though it was common by this point in China (unfortunately I was unable to follow up on any of the academic sources upon which this information seems to have been based, as I did not have institutional access to any of the relevant journals). Perhaps the fact that these pearls are suitable for grinding implies that they are not high-grade enough for jewellery, making the rhetorical question more forceful. Otherwise, it is well documented in Ayurvedic and classical Chinese sources that ground-up pearls were used for medicinal purposes (Barroso 2019, 404–405). shining with rays of light
in the pestle for flowering sugarcaneWhen sugarcane starts to flower, it is a sign that it is ready to harvest. thinking,

‘[They] threaten the beauty of our smiles.’In this topos, the normal situation is that the gift brought by the hero is unimpressive because it is easy to find nearby. Presumably this is implied by the fact that they are being ground down as higher quality pearls would have been kept intact for jewellery.

div.p: eṉpatu kaiyuṟai yeḷumai kūṟiyatu.
This is [the confidante] having told [him] about the ease [of acquisition] of the gift.

lg.l: O lord of excellent grace, we bow to you!

Nowhere on [this] mountainside,cēṇ uyar indicates that the mountain is tall even from a distance, not that it is tall and distant. One could understand the mountain as his or theirs, but I understand theirs. Following the PK source, I think one ought to read the poem sarcastically and understand that such flowers are indeed common on their mountain and such a gift is pedestrian. If genuine, the central idea is then that the confidante is impressed by such an exotic gift (a notion she expresses in poem 34 of this chapter’s commentary). tall [even] from a distance,
have we ever a leaf skirt with such fragrant flowers.

div.p: eṉpatu kaiyuṟai yemakkut takāteṉṟatu.

This is [the confidante] having said [to the hero], ‘The gift is not worthy of us.’Depending on whether one takes the poems sarcastically or genuinely, the koḷu’s meaning changes. Either the gift is not worthy of them, or vice versa. Both are possible with its wording.

lg.l: O man from the slopes of the great mountain,
after learning of the state of [her] of sweet words
and the grace of a peacock, [you] having fashioned

a soft, cool leaf skirt of flowers, I will take it.For this interpretation to work syntactically, one must take purintu as a subject-changing viṉaiyeccam. Otherwise the confidante would be the subject of puri-tal, which would require a different understanding. One could perhaps take it adverbially and in a different meaning – something along the lines of ‘with desire’.

div.p: eṉpatu talaimakaṇilaimai yaṟintu koḷkuvaṉ eṉṟatu.
This is [the confidante] having said, ‘Knowing the state of the heroine, I will take [the gift].’

lg.l: Calling it a horse, they ride the Palmyra stems.
Calling them flowers, they wear chaplets of crowded erukkam buds.
And in the streets they are shouted at.

When desire reaches its climax, they become something else.piṟitum ākupa can be understood another way: ‘When desire reaches its climax, something else will happen too.’ That lines up with the topos in the PK poems, but does not have to be the interpretation in this poem. For more discussion on this, see the footnotes to this poem in Wilden 2010.

div.p: eṉpatu maṭal ēṟuvaṉ eṉṟatu.
This is [the hero] having said, ‘I will ride the Palmyra horse.’

lg.l: Ah,The particle amma normally carries a lamentative force, but here, as the poem is the confidante’s reminder that the hero ought to be honourable, that doesn’t quite fit. It could make some sense if one understood it ironically, as a response to his threat. since you are gracious,
you will not take the wide-spread Palmyra horse

so that the great flockskiḷai here may be a play on words. It can either refer to the flocks of birds who will lose their home and cry out if the hero decides to cut down the Palmyra for his performance, or to her family members and neighbours who will cry out on seeing his performance. of birds cry out.

div.p: eṉpatu maṭal ēṟṟu vilakkiyatu.
This is [the confidante] having prevented [the hero from] mounting the Palmyra horse.

lg.l: O, is it easy for you – the way to draweḻutum āṟu can also be split as eḻutu(m) māṟu, in which case a meaning like ‘deface’ or ‘misrepresent’ would make some sense.
the young woman with the bright jewels’
parakeet-speech, her gait, or her young soft grace?

div.p: ituvum atu.
And this is that.

lg.l: Even though her friends with bright foreheads can go anywhere,
along which path can she depart –

the soft innocent daughter of those whose lives are bow-battling?The idea here is presumably to highlight the fact that her family is dangerous, and that by exposing her by riding the Palmyra horse, the hero would trap her and possibly make himself a target.

div.p: ituvum atu.
And this is that.

lg.l: Because you withstoodāṟṟi must be understood as: ‘to be able to deal with’, i.e., to survive, for this to make sense. the elephant with murderous strength
and removed ourLit.: ‘in / with regard to us’. cruel suffering,
please give [us] the leaf skirt with cool fragrant water lilies
that resembles the eyes and body of the young woman.

div.p: eṉpatu taḻai yetir kōṭal.
This is [the confidante] accepting the leaf skirt.

lg.l: O girl,aṉṉāy is the normal word for ‘mother’, but it is also used as a poetic form of address when the confidante speaks to the heroine. desiring my lies,
he will come this way again.
What are we to say to him now?

div.p: eṉpatu melitākac collik kuṟai nayappittatu.
This is [the confidante] having encouraged [the heroine] to agree to [the hero’s] request by speaking gently.

lg.l: who did not valueOne can construe this peyareccam, without attaching it to the field in the previous line. It could function as an adjective, in which case the lord might be ‘unesteemed’ or ‘dishonourable’. The structure of the poem would then be: ‘Because the dishonourable lord left, like the army seizing [it], the flock seized our field’. cool red-millet field, turned his backLiterally, he ‘gave them his back’. In the context of an army arriving, the implication must be that he surrendered and ran away. and left,
like an army of sharp spears snatching [it],
the red-beaked green flockIt is a common trope that green parrots flock around millet fields and need to be chased away. For a parallel for the phrase, see NA 134.4. have seized and taken [it].

div.p: eṉpatu nāṇoṭu nīṅkal.

This is [the heroine] leaving with bashfulness.A sense of shame here might even be a touch strong for the connotation of nāṇ. My understanding is that she becomes embarrassed, out of a sense of modesty, and deflects the conversation to something else, to not have to talk directly about the hero’s advances and their relationship.

lg.l: The man from the ghat who left in pain,
after yesterday watching a crab protecting its mate here,

– has he not returned?vantilaṉ mātō: this combination of a perfective negative form and the particle -mātō is not found in the old Tamil corpus. Other non-tense-marked negatives with -mātō can often be translated by: ‘surely x will…’. How this kind of rhetorical question is meant to work in the past tense is unclear. My mind suffers.

div.p: eṉpatu valitākac collik kuṟai nayappittatu.
This is [the confidante] having encouraged [the heroine] to agree to [the hero’s] request by speaking forcefully.

lg.l: She and I, we two are not different.

And still, without me knowing, she hid [her feelings]Presumably this means the heroine hid her feelings from her confidante; however, it could also be that she was physically hidden and that is why she was unable to manufacture their meeting.
– the celestial woman with doe-like kajal eyes from the mountain.

div.p: eṉpatu tōḻi taḻīik koṇṭatu.
This is the confidante having kindly taken [the gift].

lg.l: The man who brought [it] yesterday cast off [our] affliction
and shot the elephant with burning strength.
Won’t the leaf skirt lose its colour and wither, young woman –
difficult to pick, from the mountains with high peaks.

div.p: eṉpatu kaiyuṟai yēṟpittatu.
This is [the confidante] having entrusted the gift [to the heroine].

lg.l: Like the minds of those who encounter the nectar of true speech,

of Matitaraṉ of Vaḻuttūr,It is generally considered that the author of the TNV may have come from Vaḻuttūr or composed his treatise there, and that his teacher may have been called Matitaraṉ. For more see \S\ref{sec:authorship} of the introduction. who shines on earth

and examined things with subtlety in [his] fine composition,This need not be his own composition – he could be a teacher explaining other works, but nuṇṇiyaṟ paṉuval is not a designation for any specific text and is not attested anywhere else that I have seen.
on seeing the cool leaf skirt you brought and gifted,

the heart of the young woman who had come to accept [it]The precise connotation of vantaṉaḷ is not clear to me. As I understand it here, it indicates that the heroine’s acceptance of the gift is the result of a process of encouragement and persuasion, as suggested by the previous poems. One could take this more literally, and understand that she has come to meet the hero, or that she is one who has come to accept a meeting with the hero. Just based on where the poem falls in the akam narrative presented in this commentary, I translated as I did.

– whatyā is a late- or post-Caṅkam interrogative particle, presumably a contraction of yātu. See Tirukkuṟaḷ 54 for example. For a discussion regarding different interpretations of the different variants for this word, see the critical notes in the apparatus. state it has obtained, I have not known.I do not understand this to be a literal question, where the confidante actually does not know how her friend is feeling. The rhetorical flavour that I have tried to bring out is that the heroine’s happiness at seeing his gift is so incomparable that either the confidante has never known such happiness in her friend, or has never known such happiness herself. Considering the comparison in the poem, it would be highly unlikely for the confidante to be in an actual state of confusion. That would imply the experience of the nectar of truth was not unambiguously positive, which I think is doubtful.

div.p: eṉpatu kaiyuṟai yetirntamai kūṟiṟṟu.
This is [the confidante] having told [the hero] [how the heroine] accepted the gift.

lg.l: This flowery grove in our vast land
full of many trees with leafy branches
and which provides cover from the rain
– oh, anyone would desire it.yāvarum viḻaitakaittu could just as well mean that the grove ‘is suitable for anyone to feel desire in.’

div.p: eṉpatu pakaṟ kuṟi yiṭam uraittatu.
This is [the confidante] having spoken about the place for the daytime tryst.

lg.l: The hill of the red one with anklets and armlets,
the ground red after he felled and killed demons

with arrows with redAlternatively, ‘straight’ or ‘thick’. The repetition of ‘red’ here has rhetorical value, and presumably that is the meaning the poet primarily intended. stems and a red-tusked elephant,
has bunches of blood-red glory lilies.

div.p: eṉpatu talaimakaḷaik kuṟiyiṉkuṟi referred to both the tryst and the location of the tryst and the early theoreticians and commentators used them quite interchangeably. Perhaps later editors sought to standardise and narrow the meaning of the word into just the tryst, hence the addition of va(yiṉ). From Wilden 2006, p. 157: ‘Equally kuṟi, etymologically meaning ‘sign’, is defined by the TP and IA as the appointed meeting place of the lovers, whereas in the kiḷavi-s (and also in the poems) it refers to the meeting itself, unless it refers to the sign used to indicate the place of the meeting.’ iṟuttip peyarntatu.
This is [the confidante] having left, after placing the heroine at the meeting place.

lg.l: Did your beloved friend dress you?I understand kai as an empty auxiliary, though one could take it literally, in which case the hero would be specifying that the confidante got her ready ‘by hand’.

Without a doubt, it has come truemey peṟṟaṉṟu might refer to hypothetical beauty of the garland when fixed by the friend, which is how it is taken in the translation. Otherwise, one could understand that the garland has ‘obtained [her] body’, in the sense that it is already on her. Either way, the general sense of the poem is the same. The hero is telling the heroine that she looks as though her friend had dressed and adorned her.
as the flower garland [you] wear takes on great beauty.

div.p: eṉpatu tāṉ ṟōḻiyiṟ puṉaintamai uṇarttiyatu.
This is [the hero] having informed [the heroine that her] decoration [looks as though done] by the confidante herself.

lg.l: I am like the sun for this pure flower-chapleted one – Since the comparison in the poem is being made between the heroine and the lotus being able to stand undiminished in the face of harsh words and the harsh sun respectively, tūmalark kaṇṇi has to be taken as an aṉmoḻittokai.
she who is like a lotus,
that rose in the sapphire-watered pond to obtain beauty.
Even though I speak some heated words in haste,
[her] beauty is undiminished, because of her obtaining [me].

div.p: eṉpatu talaimakaṇilaimai kūṟiyatu.
This is [the hero] having talked about the heroine’s state.

lg.l: O splendid innocent daughter of the angry man from the forest,
you who have been decorated with a fragrant flower chaplet,

a great cool garland, a garlandThese two garlands – kōtai and piṇaiyal – must be different in some way. Perhaps in how they are strung and/or bound together. There does not seem to be a clear understanding of the difference any longer. made of jasmine buds,

and a forehead ornament made from buds,Following the advice of Dr. Indra Manuel, vāy has been translated as a postposition with the same function as -iṉ or -iliruntu (‘out of’). This is not the standard meaning at all, but it makes good sense. Another option would be to take vāy as a verbal root meaning ‘to excel’, in which case one could translate: ‘a garland upon which buds excel’ or ‘a garland which excels with buds’. should show grace.

div.p: eṉpatu koṇṭu nīṅkal. 17.
This is [the confidante] taking [the heroine] and leaving.

The C1 reading ākiyarō is relatively common as a rhetorical question in Caṅkam Tamil, employing the optative, which does not mark number or gender, in this case something like ‘what might have become of?’ (cf. KT 40, KT 49, PN 232 etc.). The question is famously posed in the first line of KT 40: yāyu ñāyum yārā kiyarō (‘My mother and your mother, what are they [to each other]’) – a variation on the question found here. Could UVC have been swayed by the parallels in the PK and TK, which have a similar-looking but different formula in their final lines – yār kaṇṇatō aṇṇal (n)iṉ aruḷē (‘upon whom, O lord, is your grace [placed]’)? The meaning is close to what we find in the TNV, but crucially kaṇṇātu-ō here is not a verbal form, but rather a nominal construction. In practice, I understand it to function like a locative marker, though it is maybe more accurately described as a pronominal derivation of the noun kaṇ (‘place’) in the neuter singular – ‘the thing whose place is’ – with an interrogative particle. This is markedly different from the C1 reading of the TNV poem, so I do not think it appropriate to emend on this basis. The emended reading yāṅku ākiyatu-ō is not attested elsewhere except in this poem, so I see no sufficiently convincing argument, as it still makes perfectly good sense.

The main rhetorical question of this anonymous poem quoted in the IAC and provided in the source layer of the apparatus of the present edition – the confidante wondering what she can tell the heroine – and the image of girls playing in the sand are shared by the TNV poem and its source. The source poem is also quoted in Nacciṉārkkiṉiyar’s commentary to TP 114, which UVC in turn provides as a parallel in a footnote for this poem in his TNV edition.

UVC does not, however, note the reading of this poem that I have found printed in the two editions of the IAC, which I have provided above in the source layer of the apparatus. One potential justification for his emendation, which I think is unnecessary, is the second line of the poem as transmitted in the TPn editions I have seen. It reads: poṟimāṇ variyalava ṉāṭṭalu māṭṭāḷ. In UVC’s edition of the TNV, the final two and a half cīr-s read the same. The reading presented in this edition follows that printed in the IAC and C1.

The most well-attested reading – yāṉilai – transmitted in C1, makes little to no sense to me. One can only split this in two ways: yāṉ nilai or yāṉ ilai. The only reasonable agent of the finite verb peṟṟanṟu is neñcam (‘the heroine’s heart’), and nilai (‘state’) is the only reasonable object. yāṉ then needs to be understood as an oblique, unmarked to preserve the vocalic mōṉai between the first acai-s of the last two lines. If so, it would make little sense that the heroine’s heart would obtain the state of the confidante (the speaker of the poem and thus the referent of yāṉ), and the final clause would make even less sense. The reasoning behind the reading printed in Cām is also slightly unclear to me. UVC must have thought that the y of yāṉ was an incorrect glide. His emendation is not, however, completely satisfactory. āṉilai can be taken in three ways: āṉ nilai (‘cow-state’ or ‘cowshed’); āṉilai (‘that state’); or āṉilai (a shrine to Śiva in Karūr). Unless obtaining the cow-state/shed was some euphemism for a positive emotion, I do not understand it. As a shrine, one could read the poem in a religious light – Matitaraṉ is one of Śiva’s epithets. The basic structure of the poem would read: ‘like the minds… where Śiva in Vaḻuttūr… the heart… obtained Āṉilai. I have not known [it].’ Here also, one understands obtaining Āṉilai to be a euphemism for something positive, presumably some religious bliss or enlightenment. Within the context of the TNV, this is unlikely. This would be the only religious poem in the whole text, and it does not seem as though this was UVC’s interpretation. He cited this poem in his introduction as potential evidence that the author of the TNV may have come from Vaḻuttūr or composed the text there, and that Matitaraṉ was his teacher. He acknowledged that the name suggested a possible Śaivite affiliation, but clearly did not read this as the primary meaning of the poem. The final interpretation is the most convincing of the three, and is the closest in sense to my suggested reading. If āṉilai is a combination of the deictic a, which has been lengthened for the sake of the metre, and nilai (‘state’), then all that would have to be modified in the translation is replacing ‘what’ with ‘that’. The meaning would remain essentially the same. This relies on an uncommon sandhi, though. There is one other attestation of this form that I have found in Peruṅkatai 25.90. In UVC’s own commentarial gloss of this occurrence, he analyses it as anta + nilai, so this was presumably also his understanding here. The misapplication of the intervocalic glide, using y instead of v, is not present anywhere else in this manuscript. All of the other witnesses also transmit a reading with initial yā, which is partially why I am inclined towards this edition’s reading. C1 also does show some confusion between ṉ and n. UVC seems to have had the same idea at some stage, as he corrected C2 to yānilai. This is no more invasive an emendation than his eventual reading in print, and I think it makes as much sense in the context of the poem, and more sense in the context of C1.
Neither of the poems bears a great resemblance to the one quoted in the TNV; however, they are certainly used to exemplify the same situation.
